title: Hard Facts and the Threshold: What the Gambia v. Myanmar Should Not Decide - Opinio Juris
content: In association with the International Commission of Jurists [His Excellency Filipo Tarakinikini is the Permanent Representative of the Republic of Fiji to the UN. He has spent more than two decades as an infantry officer and then another two in United Nations service. Geert-Jan Alexander Knoops is aprofessor of international law at the University of Amsterdam and defence counsel before the ICC, having spent more than three decades as defence counsel before the ICTY. Gregory Rose is a professor of international law at the University of Wollongong.] Note: Fiji did not intervene in The Gambia v. Myanmar. In this post we will address the doctrine rather than the outcome. The Court concluded three weeks of merits hearings in The Gambia v. Myanmar on 29 January 2026 and is now in deliberation. It is the first full merits hearing in a genocide case in more than a decade, the first in which the Court will rule on a dispute brought by a non-injured State, and the first ever ICJ genocide case deciding culpability in circumstances where there has not been a separate prior judicial finding of guilt proved beyond a reasonable doubt by an international criminal tribunal. Whatever it decides will be, for a generation, the modern law of genocide. Our concern is not with the outcome. It is with the reasoning, and specifically with how far that reasoning will be asked to travel. In April 2011, the ICTY Trial Chamber convicted Ante Gotovina after employing what became known as the “200 metre standard”. The Chamber relied on a rule it had itself established: that artillery impacts falling more than 200 metres from a legitimate military target evidenced unlawful indiscriminate shelling. The standard appeared nowhere in the evidence, in the pleadings, or in the law of armed conflict. It was constructed because the Chamber needed something to bear the weight of the inference it wished to draw. Nineteen months later the Appeals Chamber found the standard to be without foundation, and Gotovina was acquitted. The episode is worth recalling because it is the clearest modern illustration of a recurring hazard. Where the facts before a tribunal are reflecting the overwhelming complexity of urban warfare and the applicable evidentiary standard is demanding, there is a structural temptation to relieve the pressure by adjusting the standard rather than by confronting what the evidence will and will not carry. The adjustment rarely survives appellate scrutiny. But the ICJ has no appellate chamber. What it decides in Myanmar will not be legally corrected; it will be cited. Four Questions, and How Far the Answers Will Travel The questions put from the Bench during the January hearings indicate that the Court is alive to precisely the issues on which its reasoning will be most portable. First, Judge Hmoud asked whether individual criminal responsibility and State responsibility for genocide constitute distinct regimes, such that the dolus specialis required for attribution to a State differs from that required for attribution to a person. This is the most consequential question before the Court. The Convention describes genocide, in its title, its preamble and Article I, as a crime. If State responsibility for that crime can be established on a standard materially lower than the criminal standard, international criminal jurisdiction over genocide becomes superfluous. Adopting a lower evidentiary standard for State responsibility would create a strong incentive for strategic forum shopping. Applicant States could seek a finding of genocide before the ICJ rather than pursue the far more demanding criminal process before the ICC. The potential rationale for a differentiation between the evidentiary standard for a state responsibility and the standard for individual criminal responsibility, being that the latter is about the establishment of individual criminal guilt, seems not convincing.  An ICJ determination that a State committed or failed to prevent genocide would carry significant political and legal weight and open the door to subsequent criminal proceedings against individual leaders. The rationale for a differentiation between the evidentiary standard for state responsibility and for individual criminal responsibility, would then become less relevant, simply because state responsibility, findings are likely to be relied upon by prosecutors and courts as part of the broader evidentiary context for individual guilt. For that reason alone, there is no rationale for applying different standards of proof to the same allegation of genocide. Second, Judge Cleveland asked what weight should attach to NGO reports tendered in evidence. Third, Judge Gomes Robledo asked whether adverse inferences may be drawn from a respondent’s refusal to admit international investigative bodies. Both questions concern the architecture of proof, and both will be answered once, in Myanmar, for every genocide case that follows. The evidentiary question is not a technicality dressed up as principle. If reports of United Nations fact-finding missions and commissions of inquiry acquire presumptive probative status by virtue of their institutional provenance, then a body of material assembled to a standard expressly lower than any court’s — reliant on secondary sourcing, frequently unable to verify, produced under mandates that are themselves the outcome of political decision — enters the record with a weight it was never designed to carry. Bassiouni identified this problem a quarter of a century ago; it has not been solved since. The answer is not to exclude such material but to require that it be weighed individually and critically on its methodology rather than its letterhead. The same discipline should apply to reports produced by non-governmental organisations, whose missions, funding and prior advocacy positions vary enormously and are relevant to weight. The adverse-inference question carries a similar risk of over-extension. A State may decline access to an international body for reasons that have nothing to do with consciousness of guilt: for example, apprehension of methodological unreliability, of politicised mandates, of predetermined conclusions. Where the ultimate finding must rest on an inference that genocidal intent is the only reasonable inference available ignoring alternative explanations cannot bear that weight. Fourth, and underlying all of this, is Article II(c) of the Genocide Convention. “Deliberately inflicting on the group conditions of life calculated to bring about its physical destruction” is the most elastic of the enumerated acts, and it is where an expansive reading would do the most work. The words “deliberately” and “calculated” are not ornamental, rather they import the specific intent requirement into the actus reus itself. A reading that permits tragic conditions of life to infer their own intent collapses the distinction the drafters were at pains to construct. Here is the point we most want to make, and we lodge it deliberately before the judgment rather than after. The Gambia v. Myanmar concerns clearance operations directed at a denationalised, unarmed minority. There was no organised armed adversary embedded within the Rohingya population. There were no dual-use objects in contention, no combatants operating from civilian infrastructure, no question of proportionality in urban targeting. Whatever the Court holds about inferring genocidal intent on those facts is a holding about those facts. It cannot be transposed, without more, to intense urban warfare against a structured armed force that operates from within civilian infrastructure. The two situations differ not only in degree but in kind, because in urban warfare there are more likely to exist alternative explanations for civilian death that do not exist in the first. The only reasonable inference test — laid down in Bosnia in 2007 and reaffirmed in Croatia in 2015 — does its essential work precisely at that point. It asks whether any explanation other than intent to destroy the group can reasonably account for a pattern of conduct. Where a State is prosecuting an armed conflict against an embedded adversary, and has taken the precautions international humanitarian law requires, alternative explanations exist by construction. That is not a loophole. It is the test operating as designed. We say this now because a distinction drawn before a judgment is a proposition of law, and the same distinction is an excuse. We are not arguing that Myanmar should prevail, and we do not suggest that the Rohingya facts fail to meet the existing threshold. They may well satisfy it. Our submission concerns the route, not the destination. A finding of genocide reached by applying the settled dolus specialis standard rigorously to compelling evidence is the Convention working properly. A finding of genocide reached by relaxing the standard because the evidence is compelling, amounts to subverting the Convention. Equally debatable is the argument of some of the interventions before the Court in the Gaza proceedings. For instance, Ireland has invited the Court to find genocidal intent where a reasonable person would have foreseen destruction of the group as a likely consequence of a State’s conduct. Whatever the merits of that proposition as policy, it amounts to a negligence standard. Foreseeability is not intent; it is the absence of intent, supplied by construction. To adopt it would be to abolish dolus specialis while retaining the word that depends on it. The argument to adopt a “holistic” approach to interpretation of the Convention is subject to the same objection in a more general form. Articles 31 and 32 of the Vienna Convention state the customary rules, as this Court has confirmed in this very context. There is no principled basis for a bespoke interpretive method reserved for this treaty in this circumstance alone, and the effect of adopting one would be to leave the substantive content of the most serious prohibition in international law contingent on a novelty. Where a legal standard is treated as sufficiently flexible to accommodate any conclusion, adjudication ceases to constrain outcomes and begins merely to ratify them. Courts that reach that condition do not increase their authority, they exhaust it by subverting the rule of law. There is a constituency in this debate that has been almost entirely silent, and it has the most to lose. Fiji has contributed troops to United Nations operations continuously since 1978 — in Lebanon, Sinai, Iraq, Timor-Leste, Golan, and elsewhere — at a scale wholly disproportionate to its population. Professional armed forces generate After-Action Reviews as a matter of standing practice: contemporaneous records produced for command accountability and legal compliance, not for litigation. If such records are treated as inherently self-serving while UN institutionally produced reports are treated as presumptively more reliable, the incentive to generate After-Action Reviews honestly, or at all, degrades. This is a legal danger to every professional military that takes compliance seriously, and it falls hardest on those that document most carefully. The second consequence is more direct. If a State that volunteers forces for an international operation — to disarm an armed group, to stabilise a collapsed authority — thereby exposes itself to genocide proceedings brought by that group’s patrons, small troop-contributing States will conclude that the risk is not worth carrying. They will not announce this. They will simply stop offering. The Convention was not drafted to produce that result, and a Court that produces it will have weakened the prevention of atrocity in the name of its punishment. The reason that five genocide cases have been brought before the Court in the past seven years, but only two cases in the first 50 years of the Genocide Convention, might be a signal that the genocide jurisdiction can be misused to get around the fact that the Court has no jurisdiction over armed conflict. The threshold for genocide is high because the word means something specific and serious. Every dilution offered is paid for by the next case, and the one after that, in which the word is asked to do work it can no longer do. Genocide law is prescribed and the Court should apply the standard it has. It should not adjust it because the facts are terrible. That the facts are terrible is precisely when the standard is worth having. ©  Opinio Juris | Design by Open & Honest | In association with the International Commission of Jurists

title: Blizzard Entertainment Announced Diablo V - 80 Level
content:
During BlizzCon 2026, the development team revealed the first details of the world. Blizzard Entertainment announced its latest addition to the iconic Diablo series during BlizzCon 2026. Initially, the team was considering an expansion to the latest title – Diablo IV. However, with the creative ambition they had for the new title, they ultimately decided to make it into a full, separate installment in the Diablo series. "Do we do this as an expansion to Diablo IV, or do we do this as a sequel? Sequels allow us to do something really special to a game, especially a long-standing game like Diablo where we can get in and really change the fundamentals of what the game is. And it's really hard to do when you're building on top of a game that's been around for several years, has had several expansions and seasons," said Matt Zitterman, Diablo V executive producer. The new game is set 100 years after the events of Diablo IV. After Elias and Lilith died, Sanctuary descended into the apocalypse. Diablo, the Lord of Terror, finally won and took over the human world, getting a step closer to invading the Heavens. The Lord of Terror is present from the beginning, guiding the plot of the game. In the new chapter, you'll become the Heir to Westmarch, and you'll need to build an army of allies willing to push the Lord of Terror off his throne. The developers hinted at complex, thoughtfully written storylines by saying that the allies who join you on this journey to dethrone Diablo are "fascinating characters with pasts, stakes, and scars from surviving in Diablo’s Sanctuary." The new environments are going to be eye candy for those who love gloomy, depressing, post-apocalyptic scenery. In Blizzard's words, Sanctuary under Diablo's rule is a "haunting, desolate land shaped by despair". The world in the new game is a procedural landscape that is constantly changing, and you'll have to find a way around it. During BlizzCon, the developers announced the first three character classes in the new game: Demon Hunter, Monk, and Plague Knight. The Demon Hunter attacks from the shadows and leaps across the battlefield as they demolish their victims. The Monk is the master of martial arts, fighting evil creatures with fists and using holy power to defeat their enemies. The Plague Knight is a walking death trap – they spread fatal disease as they move through the battlefield. When it comes to items, Diablo V's itemization is largely influenced by that of Diablo II. Inventory is your holy grail, determining how you make use of your arsenal. Plus, in Diablo V, we'll see the return of gear-based sets. Diablo II-inspired Runes and Runewords will be there to make it easier to browse through all of your boosts. The previous installment in the series broke Blizzard's sales record, becoming its fastest-selling title ever. It gained extremely positive reviews from both critics and gamers. However, with the recent release of the Lord of Hatred DLC, Steam reviews started to go down rapidly, since players were not thrilled to discover that, suddenly, the game they purchased at full price became basically unplayable without the DLC. Blizzard's DLC policy for the new title is unknown, but since they are looking to take players' feedback into consideration throughout development, we might expect fairer access to the game and more transparent pricing. As the company stated, Diablo V is still in its early developmental stages. Starting next year, Blizzard is planning to share regular updates on the process, throwing in some new details and revealing new game features every now and then. The company is planning to release the game in spring 2029. What's more, just a year later, Blizzard is going to release a new StarCraft game, which they also teased at BlizzCon 2026. title: Diablo V Promises More Classes Than Any Previous Diablo Game, as Blizzard Brings Back Procedural Overworlds and Diablo II Runewords - Wccftech
content:
Blizzard's most surprising reveal at BlizzCon 2026 was undoubtedly the announcement of Diablo V, of which we had had no rumors prior to the Opening Ceremony. Even more interesting is the fact that Diablo V won't be about stopping the titular Lord of Terror, but about what happens after he's already taken Sanctuary. That premise had fans excited about this twist, and the ‘Forging the Next Era’ panel offered them plenty of details about the project due in Spring 2029. The panel featured Blizzard president Johanna Faries as the host, while Senior Game Director Joe Shely, Senior Production Director Tiffany Wat, Senior Art Director John Mueller, Narrative Director Jennifer Hepler, and Executive Producer Matt Zitterman spoke about the game. The team began by breaking down the Diablo player base after 30 years, looking for the clusters within it: players there for the story and dark fantasy atmosphere, players there to grind bosses and min-max builds, and everyone in between. The goal was for every feature to be anchored to the kind of Diablo player it was primarily for. From there, they looked hard at Diablo IV, what worked, how it had evolved in response to feedback, and where they wanted to try something genuinely new. That conversation led to the expansion-versus-sequel question, and the answer came down to fundamentals. A sequel lets them change what the game fundamentally is, which is extremely difficult on top of a title several years, expansions, and seasons deep. There was also the small matter of the franchise's big bad himself. As Zitterman put it, Mephisto and Lilith were epic characters with real depth in Diablo IV and its expansions, and Diablo deserves that and more. Narrative director Jennifer Hepler laid out the central premise: for 30 years, players have been scrambling to protect Sanctuary before Diablo could rise. In Diablo V, other heroes rose to stop him, and they failed. The players will be living in the aftermath of what they failed to prevent. When the game begins, seven years will have passed since Diablo conquered Sanctuary. He now rules from the throne of Westmarch, wielding humanity's people and souls as weapons in the Eternal Conflict, with the conquest intended as a stepping stone toward his ultimate goal of invading the Heavens. The Western Continent has become an outpost of Hell. Few humans remain who haven't bowed or joined the cults, and a terrifying handful of powerful humans have been corrupted and elevated into Dread Commanders, wielding power rivaling the dukes of Hell. Anyone who resists ends up in a soul cage or is dragged into the Terror Realm, Diablo's personal corner of Hell. The player character is the Heir to Westmarch, and the story begins when they discover they can enter the Terror Realm and survive. Hepler was also firm on one point: the team briefly explored making Diablo a morally grey figure, given Blizzard's track record with Sylvanas and Lilith, but kept arriving at the same conclusion. Diablo is Diablo. He isn't redeemable or misunderstood. The question isn't whether he has a point, but what happens now that he's won. However, just like with Lilith, the player character has a mysterious personal connection to Diablo, revealed over the course of the game, which makes them both a genuine threat to him and uniquely vulnerable to his influence. Here's the significant headline mechanical change: procedural generation is back in both dungeons and the overworld. Tiffany Wat explained that the Dread Commanders are actively reshaping the land, a process the team affectionately calls Terror Forming. Returning to a region visited before, players could find the landmarks, terrain, monsters and rewards to be all different. The knock-on effect is that the knowledge accumulated yesterday does not necessarily help the player today. Joe Shely's pitch to his own team is that players should never feel quite safe, which is easier to achieve when all the towns are gone. Art director John Mueller described three visual lenses the team works through. The past covers everything lost, a life-after-people vision of a desolate Sanctuary. The present is where evil has touched the world, where the Dread Commanders have burned through, leaving something strange behind. The future is what the player hero will be trying to prevent: Hell breaking through entirely. Each Dread Commander brings their own distinct visual theme to the land they've corrupted. With every settlement already destroyed in this post-apocalyptic version of Sanctuary, Blizzard needed a new answer to the question of where safety lives. The solution is the caravan. Rather than moving between towns, players bring a traveling band of wagons and followers with them. The caravan grows upon meeting other survivors, and its members become merchants, crafters and companions. Zitterman compared the feeling to the Rogue Encampment in the original Diablo: humanity eking out a corner of safety, gathered around a campfire as the last bastion against the dark. The design consequence is more interesting than it first appears. There are no ordinary civilians left in Sanctuary, which means no quest givers waiting by the roadside. All side content, therefore, comes from the caravan members, and every quest is part of the personal story of someone brought along. Two companions were teased. Blizzard confirmed a former Sister of the Sightless Eye, and the panel spent rather longer on a treasure goblin named Zarg, who is joining up simply because he understands that the player character is considerably easier to steal from than Diablo is. Joe Shely announced the first three classes that will be in Diablo V: The big claim is that Diablo V will launch with more classes than any previous Diablo game, and Joe specified he means more total classes, not just more at ship than a given entry had at its own launch. The game's itemization pillars are depth, clarity, and identity, and the whole approach is explicitly inspired by Diablo II. Items start simple and grow with the player. Large items once again occupy multiple inventory slots, which the art team is enjoying for the bigger icons and the familiarity. Controller players worried about manipulating a grid inventory were assured that the team has solutions in mind. Gear-based sets are returning, too. The team liked what the talisman did in the Lord of Hatred expansion for Diablo IV, but wanted to reattach the set concept to gear itself, because picking up one piece and recognizing it as part of a larger whole creates its own quest. They also say they have ideas for making sets broaden the range of viable builds rather than narrowing them. Blizzard's official write-up adds something the panel didn't state outright: the crafting system will be rich and deep, inspired by Lord of Hatred's approach, and will include Diablo II-style Runes and Runewords. Finally, the team is experimenting with stat requirements for items, though that isn't confirmed yet. Zitterman was upfront about why Blizzard is announcing a game that's still years out: they want community feedback as early as possible, and want players involved in the process rather than presented with a finished product. Regular updates are set to begin next year, with Blizzard already collecting sign-ups on the official website in the meantime. title: Infineon RISC-V for Automotive at Hot Chips 2026 - ServeTheHome
content: Since we covered many of the other talks, we also had a draft of the Infineon RISC-V for Automotive talk for Hot Chips 2026 ready. We figured, why not give this talk some exposure too? Let us get to it. Infineon opened with the compute demands facing automotive microcontrollers. Chassis, powertrain, and ADAS applications together want real-time low latency, power efficiency, and security on top of the highest integrity levels and functional safety, all on a single part. Architecture work starts with the move from domain architecture toward zone control units and eventually full car computers. Former domain controllers evolve into central car computers handling ADAS, infotainment, and vehicle motion, while body and comfort functions consolidate into zones that share wiring and cut harness weight and cost. In automotive, the wiring harness is a huge deal. Infineon lays out the real-time areas that every automotive part must handle. Fast control loops such as E-motor control need deadlines under 10 ms and interrupt latencies in the tens of nanoseconds, while strategic functions like vehicle management tolerate multiple seconds and 10 ms interrupt latency. We heard some of this in the Waymo Sensor Fusion Processor at Hot Chips 2026 talk. With zone architecture in place, the open question is how much intelligence each zone controller should carry. Path A uses optimized multi-domain zone controllers that partially consolidate endpoint ECUs and support local power distribution, while Path B keeps zone controllers as low-complexity I/O aggregators with no intelligence of their own. Infineon says that Option A is the more advantageous path. Keeping local tactics and latency-sensitive control loops in the zone while global strategies and OEM value sit in the central compute shrinks the vehicle attack surface, eases maintenance, and cuts system cost by consolidating endpoint ECUs and decentralizing power distribution. Real zone controllers integrate workloads with very different compute demands. Real-time control, DSP and AI inference, low-power service layers, and audio processing all land on one part, so the compute architecture must scale across high-end multi-domain zones and low-end body zones while still delivering good power, performance, and area. A super-integrated zone controller pushes heterogeneity further by adding an MPU island alongside the MCU. Offloading non-real-time critical workloads to a POSIX adaptive software stack frees the real-time core, enables faster boot and wake than a full SoC, and helps a zone scale from L2 toward L2+ and L3. Against that backdrop, Infineon makes the case for RISC-V, which feels a bit like RISC-V over Arm given many of the other solutions out there. A single open and scalable ISA avoids IP-level lock-in, eases knowledge sharing, and brings ecosystem synergies across automotive, IoT, and industrial use. Standardization depends on the right profiles. Within the RVI AUTO-SIG discussion, Infineon argues the distinction is less about auto versus non-auto and more about defining industry-grade safety- and security-related products, starting from a base such as RV32E and I plus M and U and adding optionalities for supervisor mode, floating point, vectors, and hypervisor support. If you want to learn more about profiles there was an Update on RISC-V Standards and Adoption at Hot Chips 2026. Scalability depends as much on the software stack as on the ISA. Infineon points to virtualization as a key requirement so an RVM-based system can host multiple workloads and software domains cleanly. RISC-V specifies the ISA rather than implementation details. Instruction latency, memory hierarchy, cache coherency, and functional safety features such as lock-step and error tracking stay in the hands of the silicon designer, which is where automotive differentiation happens. Infineon says that in practice, detailed ISA aspects matter less than microarchitectural optimization, and for MCUs the winning attributes are memory, connectivity, specific hardware, sourcing, and final BOM cost, with the availability of automotive-qualified toolchains deciding who succeeds. Infineon closes by tying RISC-V to concrete zone controller roles. RISC-V can accelerate zone control units, but application and cost fit are driven by factors beyond the ISA, such as SoC architecture, ecosystem enablement, and ease of deployment, and long-term adoption depends on standardized hardware-software interfaces and toolchain support. That mix of open ISA freedom and the need for dependable, toolchain-backed automotive silicon frames where RISC-V fits as zone architectures mature. Infineon frames RISC-V as an ISA that removes the lock-in, but the market will be won on auto-qualified toolchains, SoC architecture, and ecosystem enablement rather than the instruction set alone. Hopefully, the automotive folks are able to support multiple ISAs unless one clearly pulls ahead. This was another neat talk, but probably one that was a bit less traditional STH coverage area focused. Interesting to see Infineon pushing RISC-V for automotive. title: Pollock: Bills v Texans Prediction - the wellsville sun
content: Joe Brady will get a major test in his first game as Bills head coach. Buffalo’s former offensive coordinator replaces the fired Sean McDermott for this afternoon’s game at Houston’s NRG Stadium (1 o’clock, CBS-TV, Bills Radio Network). Brady’s offense will be charged with facing the defending No. 1 NFL defense. He’ll be on the sideline calling offensive plays while defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard will be in the same place doing a similar chore for his unit. Buffalo’s offensive advantage is former NFL MVP Josh Allen at quarterback paired with league defending rushing champion, RB James Cook. They figure to get a lift from former Panther and Bear, D.J. Moore at wideout. The Bills’ problem is defense where the lack of depth renders it a decidedly pedestrian unit even though Buffalo is favored by 1 1/2 points. For the Texans, pass-rush specialist Will Anderson has missed the last two practices before participating in Saturday’s walk-through and he’s supposedly healthy. WHEN ASKED about his first game as an NFL head coach, Brady allowed he hasn’t contemplated the consequences. “I’ve got enough on my plate game-planning and trying to lead a football team. It’ll never be about me.” He added, “All I care about is doing what the heck we have to do to go 1-0. It’s so cliche and coachspeak … but it’s who we are. It doesn’t have to look good, it doesn’t have to be pretty. “Just put the ball down and play the next one and do what we have to do to get one more point than them.” (Chuck Pollock, a Wellsville Sun and Olean Star senior sports columnist, can be reached at cpollock@wnynet.net.) title: Predicted Newcastle United team v Leeds United with three changes - Yahoo Sports
content: Looking at this Newcastle United team v Leeds United. Matthias Jaissle having made an excellent start to his NUFC career. Only starting work five weeks ago, the new Newcastle United boss having overseen three wins and two draws in his opening five competitive United matches. In the Premier League, a win over Tottenham and draws against Liverpool and Bournemouth. Plus progress to the last 16 of the Carabao Cup thanks to wins over West Brom and Millwall. Matthias Jaissle's side aiming to now make it eight points from a possible twelve as they take on Leeds at 8pm on Monday night. As a reminder, this was the Newcastle team v Millwall on Tuesday night: Hornicek, Dedic, Schar, Botman, Hall, Ramsey, Gonzalez, Willock, Barnes, Murphy, Wissa Matthias Jaissle made three changes from the 2-2 draw against Bournemouth, with Schar, Murphy and Ramsey replacing Thiaw, Elanga and Lewis Miley. For Monday night it appears that William Osula and Dan Burn will both definitely be missing. However, we could potentially see both Joelinton and Ewen Jaouen available once again. Amar Dedic was subbed off at half-time on Tuesday night with Matthias Jaissle describing it as having done so as a precaution, due to the right-back having felt something with his hamstring. Tino Livramento was his half-time replacement but ahead of the Millwall match the manager had said that Tino wasn't going to be considered yet as starter due to still recovering from a long-term injury. Taking all of that into consideration, in my opinion…. This is my predicted Newcastle United team v Leeds United: Hornicek, Dedic, Thiaw, Botman, Hall, Lewis Miley, Gonzalez, Elanga, Barnes, Willock, Wissa If my prediction proved correct, this would be Matthias Jaissle reverting back to the eleven that started against both Spus and Bournemouth. Elanga will come back in for sure, especially as Murphy was poor at Millwall. Jacob Ramsey did okay in midweek but Lewis Miley set to come back into the team in my opinion. The same with Malick Thiaw. Fabian Schar was one of the best performers at Millwall but the Germany international is now first choice. At right-back I think it all revolves around Amar Dedic. If he is fit then I think he starts, if not then it will be Tino Livramento if Matthias Jaissle judges him now fully ready to start matches again. If the manager decided that he couldn't play either of the pair, he then of course also has the option of playing Lewis Miley at right-back. The midfielder filled in brilliantly there for a run of games last season and the United boss has the likes of Ramsey, Steur, Aladji and potentially Joelinton that he could play alongside Gonzalez in midfield. Matias Fernandez-Pardo is the other big talking point. Only a matter of time before he is starting regularly. Matthias Jaissle has said he will only play MFP when he things the 21-year-old is ready to do so. The manager clearly wants pace up top and ideally have Yoane Wissa playing behind a centre-forward, so if Osula had been available then I think he would be in that main striker role. MFP can play any position across the forward line and he has blinding pace, on balance though I think Matthias Jaissle will use him off the bench for a while longer.

New Jersey prospects kick off their two-game Rookie Showcase against the Islanders as the home team at RWJBarnabas Health Hockey House on Sunday afternoon. Puck drop is 2 p.m. ET. Anton Silaev makes his Rookie Showcase debut on Sunday. It didn’t take long for the Devils rookies to shift from practice mode to game mode. After just one day of practice, the Devils will welcome the Islanders to RWJBarnabas Health Hockey House on Sunday for the first of two Rookie Camp showcase games between the clubs. Puck drop is set for 2 p.m., with the game available to stream live on livestreamed on the Devils' official website. For the rookies, it’s an opportunity to take everything they’ve worked on over the first day of camp and put it into game action and make a quick impression. With a mix of returning prospects, recent draft picks and players looking to make an impression, Sunday’s matchup will offer the first chance to see how the group comes together when the competition ramps up. The Devils have just a single first-round pick on its roster with Anton Silaev making his debut. He was drafted 10th overall in 2024. The roster also has two second-round picks, both with NHL experience, Seamus Casey and Lenni Hämeenaho. The roster includes four fourth-round picks, three sixth rounders, one seventh and three free agent invites. For the Islanders, they boast three first-round picks, including two of their 2025 first rounders in Victor Eklund (16th overall) and Kashawn Aitcheson (17th overall). The Islanders have two second-round picks, two third and fourth round picks, a fifth and seventh round pick as well as several undrafted players as the makeup of their 25-man roster. The showcase game is one of two games the rookies will play this Rookie Camp, both against the Islanders. The Devils will visit the Isles on Tuesday. Sunday marks the Rookie Camp debut of 2024 first-round pick defenseman Anton Silaev. The 20-year-old stands at 6-foot-7 and towers over his teammates, but perhaps what stands out most is how smoothly he moves for a player of his size. Silaev's skating is a major part of his game. He covers a lot of ice and has the mobility to close gaps quickly. He has a long reach that can make life difficult for opposing forwards, and his size gives him plenty of upside as he starts to adjust to the North American game. Silaev was paired with Seamus Casey during the club's practice on Saturday, and the two are expected to be paired together against the Islanders. It'll be an interesting first look at Silaev in a game setting and, for Devils fans, a chance to see what that combination of size, skating and puck-moving ability looks like against competition. Eiserman is a 20-year-old forward with aspirations of making a push for a roster spot on the Islanders. He was selected 10 spots after Silaev, 20th overall in 2024, by New York. He has a bit of AHL experience after finishing out his Boston University career, playing 12 games with Bridgeport last season. Eiserman owns a pretty wicked NHL-caliber shot and has always been known for his ability to score goals, putting up 72 goals in 58 games during his final season with the USNTDP. He'll be looking to turn that scoring touch into an NHL opportunity this season, and with another year of development under his belt, he'll be one of the younger players in the Islanders' mix pushing for a spot. title: Big Tigger returns to V-103 morning show after criminal charges cleared - FOX 5 Atlanta
content: Big Tigger speaks onstage during Day 1 of One MusicFest at Piedmont Park on October 28, 2023 in Atlanta, Georgia. (Photo by Aaron J. Thornton/FilmMagic) ATLANTA - Atlanta radio host Darian "Big Tigger" Morgan will return to the V-103 airwaves after he was cleared of all criminal charges in a previous domestic violence case involving his estranged wife. Station officials at V-103 confirmed Morgan will resume his role hosting "The Big Tigger Morning Show" alongside co-host Francesca Amiker weekdays from 6 a.m. to 10 a.m. The move follows a multi-month absence from the program that had generated interest among listeners. Big Tigger, a long-standing voice in local radio and entertainment, is expected to step back into his primary role on the broadcast on Monday, Sept. 14. The legal battle began after Morgan was arrested in June by Sandy Springs police following a May domestic dispute involving his estranged wife, Alicia Brown. Brown accused Morgan of pushing her into a door and causing a facial injury, leading to initial charges of aggravated battery and third-degree cruelty to children. Morgan consistently denied the allegations. The Fulton County District Attorney's Office later declined to prosecute the case. PREVIOUS STORY: Big Tigger won't face charges in domestic violence case The dispute extended into broader legal matters between the former couple. In July, Brown was arrested on Interstate 85 in Hart County after law enforcement flagged an active warrant. Brown subsequently filed a federal lawsuit against Fulton County Sheriff Patrick Labat and the Fulton County Sheriff's Office, alleging the arrest was unlawful and questioning communications between Morgan and law enforcement. Additionally, Morgan's morning co-host, Francesca Amiker, filed a separate federal defamation lawsuit against Brown. title: He Bought a Cadillac CT5-V Blackwing, Drove 3,800 Miles, Is Selling It Because He Hates the Color - autoevolution

The 2026 Cadillac CT5-V Blackwing is finished in Deep Space Metallic, an option costing $625, over a Sky Cool Gray and Jet Black interior and rides on 19-inch wheels in Satin Graphite Dark Finish. So what is not to like about it? However, the owner hates it. "I am more of an orange, yellow, Kawasaki Green guy," he explains. Why didn't he buy a Cadillac CT5-V Blackwing in one of those colors in the first place? He says he practically begged Cadillac to sell him a car painted a color that was not on their list, but his request was met with multiple NOs. However, he wanted a Blackwing because it was the final high-performance car with a stick shift before Cadillac pulled the plug on it. Several months after the car was delivered to him, the automaker came up with the Curated program, which offered 160 colors to choose from. Well, wealthy or not, a brand-new Cadillac CT5-V Blackwing starts at $100,695 before checking the box for the optional Precision Package that this car comes with or the custom orange paint that his next car will wear. The Precision Package is a $18,000 option on the Cadillac CT5-V Blackwing. It doesn't add extra oomph, but it completely overhauls the car's suspension, alignment capability, and braking performance to cut down lap times. The owner says he road-tripped the Caddy to the Circuit of the Americas in Austin, Texas, for the WEC race last year, adding approximately 2,000 miles. For the rest, he just poked around town or went to car meets on Thursdays. That is what makes it rocket from 0 to 60 mph (0 to 97 kph) in 3.6 seconds when equipped with the six-speed manual transmission like this car is. The one with the auto box is 0.2 seconds quicker. It takes 11.7 seconds down the quarter mile and hits a top speed of 200 mph (322 kph). An electronic limited-slip differential and the Magnetic Ride Control are part of the plan to make the performance sedan easier to maneuver and more comfortable to ride in. An Ultra View sunroof shelters the cabin, which hosts heated and ventilated front seats. An HD Surround Vision camera provides the soundtrack when the driver has had enough of the V8 supercharged orchestra. Even if it is still a new car, it still comes with some flaws, and the most annoying one is the fact that the seat massagers on the bolsters and lumbar adjustment functions on the front seats are inoperative. He explains that he just didn’t want to argue with Cadillac or explain why there is interior damage on the car that he was planning to sell anyway. So, this is something that the buyer will have to solve. The list of flaws also includes indentation above the front grille, some missing windshield gasket top pieces that he has no idea how he lost, and the fact that the gauges occasionally reset from Track to Tour mode. The car came from the factory wearing the Michelin Pilot Sport Cup 2R tires, but the owner swapped them for Pilot Sport 4S units at 222 miles (357 kilometers). The previous ones were terrible in the rain, he complains. The engine oil and filter were changed earlier this month at 3,786 miles. The front view camera, steering column lock module, nd ttelamtics control module were reprogrammed in June 2026. All four tires were replaced in August 2025. The window sticker indicates that the original owner, the man selling it now, paid $125,110 to drive it off the showroom floor. Now, with six days to go to the end of the auction, the highest bid sits at $86,000 and counting. The one who places the winning bid will also get two keys, service records, lug nuts and a key, two foam brake rotor protectors, a tire inflator, and the tow eyebolt, along with a clean Carfax report showing no accidents or mileage discrepancies. Lots of writing, testdrives, traveling, off-road driving courses, track driving courses, defensive driving courses and diplomas. title: Diablo V: Forging the Next Era - Blizzard News
content:
Igniting our celebration of 30 years, we unveiled the Diablo V: Forging the Next Era panel at BlizzCon 2026. The development team revealed the first details of the world, classes, and systems taking shape in Diablo V. You’ll become the Heir to Westmarch and traverse a Sanctuary actively reshaped by Diablo, accompanied by a growing caravan of survivors. The team also unveiled the Demon Hunter, Monk, and all-new Plague Knight classes and shared how past Diablo games are inspiring a renewed focus on item depth, clarity, and identity. These early ideas all flow from the central premise at the heart of Diablo V: the heroes of the past have failed, Sanctuary has fallen, and Diablo has won. This is the foundation for Diablo’s next era, and only the beginning of what the team plans to share as development continues. Catch up on the full Diablo V: Forging the Next Era panel here: Diablo has conquered Sanctuary, a stepping stone to invading the Heavens. Now from the throne of Westmarch, he wields Sanctuary's people and souls as weapons in the Eternal Conflict. Diablo is no longer a distant threat waiting at the end of the journey. He is present from the moment Diablo V begins, shaping the story, the world, and your path through it. As Heir to Westmarch, on the run through the charred remains of a kingdom now transformed into an outpost of Hell. Few humans have escaped Diablo’s rule. Some have bowed before him or joined his cults, while a terrifying few have been corrupted into Dread Commanders and raised to rival the powers of Hell. Your mysterious connection to Diablo makes you both a threat and uniquely vulnerable to his powerful influence. With Sanctuary’s greatest champions gone, what must you become to fight for the home taken from you? This is not Sanctuary waiting for the apocalypse. It is already living through one. In Diablo V, humanity has fallen into ruin, and the Western Continent is at the heart of Diablo’s reign of terror. We revealed a haunting, desolate land shaped by despair, resilience, and the few survivors fighting to endure another day. Sanctuary itself is no longer stable. Diablo is actively reshaping the world through terror, reflected by a procedural landscape where terrain, points of interest, monsters, and reward can change when you return. It’s ruins tell the story of what was lost, its corruption reveals Diablo’s present rule, and the encroaching forces of Hell offer a glimpse of what comes next. With Sanctuary under Diablo’s rule, survival is no longer tied to towns or conquered strongholds. Instead, you’ll need to build a caravan of allies who travel with you through the scorched wastes. These allies will be both vendors and steadfast companions, a growing community full of stories to discover. They are fascinating characters with pasts, stakes, and scars from surviving in Diablo’s Sanctuary. Amongst your newfound companions are a former Sister of the Sightless Eye... and a stranded Treasure Goblin searching for meaning in a world where greed has lost its purpose. The team offered an early look at how they’re thinking about class identity, progression, and loot. During the panel, we revealed the first three classes coming to Diablo V: The Demon Hunter returns to stalk the forces of Hell with twin crossbows, striking from the shadows and leaping across the battlefield to annihilate their prey. The Monk brings martial perfection back to Sanctuary, battering demons to a pulp with fists and calling down holy power to smite those who stand in their path. The all-new Plague Knight is the embodiment of walking death. They roam the battlefield, spreading disease and pestilence, ultimately consuming it for power. These are only the first of the classes we’ll reveal on the road to Diablo V, with more details on their combat, progression, and build possibilities to come. The team emphasized their goal is to design items to feel readable, memorable, and worth chasing across hundreds of hours. Itemization in Diablo V is inspired by Diablo II. We’re experimenting with stat requirements on gear. Your inventory plays a key role in how you wield your arsenal, larger items once again take up more slots in your inventory. Gear-based sets are also returning for Diablo V. This will be a rich and deep crafting system, inspired by Lord of Hatred’s approach, with Diablo II-style Runes and Runewords. Diablo V is still early in development, and this reveal marks the beginning of an ongoing conversation with the Diablo player community. Starting in 2027, we plan to share regular updates offering a closer look at our progress, the ideas guiding development, and features taking shape along the way. Bringing players into the process early gives us the opportunity to listen, understand what excites you the most, and allow that to inform the decisions ahead. We want to build a Diablo game that honors what players love while taking the series somewhere genuinely new. The next era has only begun. Sign up for future updates at Diablo5.Blizzard.com. title: Diablo V First Look: Blizzard’s Next Sequel Doubles Down on Darkness - Esquire
content: Only three years after Diablo IV, Blizzard reveals the next sequel of its hit RPG series exclusively to Esquire. The end is now. Three and a half years after Diablo IV, Blizzard Entertainment is announcing the next installment in its popular action role-playing series: Diablo V. For the first time in more than 15 years, players will square off with the Big D himself, Diablo, who has changed quite a bit since he rose as the ultimate Prime Evil. Diablo V is scheduled to launch in 2029 on platforms Blizzard has yet to announce. “You’re entering Diablo V with Sanctuary in an apocalypse,” says Joe Shely, senior game director, in an exclusive interview with Esquire. “Sanctuary is not a happy place in the best of times, but Diablo V takes it to another level. You’re living in a world that has been overrun by Diablo. He sits on the throne, humanity is destroyed, and players themselves are on the run.” “You’ve spent the last 30 years fending off the apocalypse,” adds Jennifer Hepler, narrative director of Diablo V. “We were like, What if Diablo won and we scramble to claw back territory by our fingernails? We wanted to make a world that’s darker than ever but give you a reason to fight for it.” Ahead of the game’s reveal at BlizzCon in Anaheim, California, Esquire sat down with members of the game’s senior development team, who peeled back the curtain on players’ next adventure across Sanctuary as it has fallen under Diablo’s occupation. Next to Shely and Hepler is John Mueller, Diablo V’s senior art director. Together they tell Esquire that the driving question behind the new project was “Wouldn’t it be cool if…?” Wouldn’t it be cool if … we brought back fan-favorite classes? Wouldn’t it be cool if … there was a single memorable space full of interesting people? Wouldn’t it be cool if … the story was centered entirely on the players’ characters? These questions drove Blizzard to pursue a full-fledged entry in the mainline series. Usually a new game coming a few years after the previous installment isn’t so earth-shattering for a hit video game series. But Diablo is not an ordinary series. Since Diablo II was released in 2000, fans have spent literal decades waiting for just a glimpse of sequels like Diablo III (released in 2012) and Diablo IV (released in 2023). Waiting out epochs is routine for fans. But all their waiting and wondering for what’s next ends now. What’s next is a heated reunion with Diablo. Esquire has the first-ever exclusive look at Diablo V with its concept art below. “We wanted to turn back to the title villain, who we haven’t seen in over ten years, since Diablo III,” says Shely. “He needs his own game. There are things we can do, in terms of innovations and how we tell the story, that give us a fresh slate.” Set a century after Diablo IV, Diablo V casts players as the runaway heir to the lost kingdom of Westmarch. They share a mysterious connection with Diablo, who has since evolved from a big, bad guy of fire and brimstone into a more calculated antagonist. “We wanted to give players a lot of agency in the story,” explains Hepler, the main architect of Diablo V’s story. In contrast to how players spend time in Diablo IV forging connections with Lilith and Mephisto, Hepler says they wanted players to feel their bonds “much faster” in Diablo V. “The story starts when you find you’re the only one who can go into Diablo’s terror realm and come back alive,” she says. “We wanted to give you that core identity we could build the story around. You’re not a wanderer in someone else’s story.” Hepler adds: “In past games, Diablo was brutish. What did Diablo learn from watching Mephisto? Diablo has learned how to be subtle. He is the Lord of Terror; what does terror mean? What does someone whose entire existence is provoking or feeding on fear going to be like? We want to give you that bond with him from the beginning. Why is Diablo interested in you? How you define yourself in the shadow of, and in opposition to, Diablo is a big part of the game. He is trying to control you. What do you do to push back?” Hepler clarifies that players still retain plenty of individual customization over their characters, like in their character classes. “You aren’t a fixed character. This is not Nathan Drake. This is still an ARPG. The Heir to Westmarch in your world is whatever gender and class you pick.” “You’ll shape who you are as a character, as the heir, more freely than you ever have before,” adds Joe Shely. “The idea of who you are as a person and what class you’re playing are independent in a way they’ve never been before. You can look and be whoever you want.” Speaking of classes, Shely says Diablo V “will launch with more classes than we ever had in a Diablo game before.” While the team cannot unpack each class in detail yet, it is revealing three in particular: the returning Monk and Demon Hunter, as well as the new Plague Knight. “The Monk and Demon Hunter are really established fantasies for us,” says John Mueller, who oversees the art direction of Diablo V. “The last time players saw these was Diablo III. In 2012, technology was different. We have advanced through Diablo IV, so we want to give people the best versions of these in 2029.” Shely lays out the Demon Hunter’s and Monk’s individual vibes, in case you weren’t around for Diablo III. “A Demon Hunter has light armor and twin crossbows. They’re extremely agile, pinning demons against walls. It’s a fantasy players are familiar with. And Monk, you know, who doesn’t like pulverizing demons with their fist? It’s an up-close melee class.” Then there’s the Plague Knight, a new control-based character built like a tank that spreads disease. “This is a heavily armored, ‘walking death’ character who will spread disease across the battlefield and consume that disease for power.” Artistically, the team designed the Plague Knight like a medieval iron maiden on two legs. As in any action RPG, players start the game with almost nothing. Over time, they meet new allies who join their nomadic caravan as it roves through a desolate Sanctuary. Blizzard says the caravan serves as the players’ main hub—the only “safe space” in a hellish world—and that it will physically evolve as players progress through the story. “We need there to be something you love about this world,” says Hepler. “Gathering survivors is one of the mechanisms of the story. We’re going through lands where almost everybody is dead or surrendered to Diablo. Now and then we meet a person who has held out, and they become part of the caravan. Your vendors, your craftspeople, everyone who is part of your journey are survivors. These are the people you’re fighting to protect and the source of all your side content.” Hepler reveals that the caravan will change over time as players find new survivors and level up. “Each wagon reflects their personality and background. The wagons upgrade as you go on, reflecting things you’ve done in the story. Trophies from victories appear at the campsite. It becomes a really dynamic place that tracks you in the game.” Adds Mueller, “You start this ragtag [operation]. It’s a shoddy situation. By the end, you’ve grown that into a very aspirational space you love going back to. We think that’s going to be a fun, dynamic way to experience the story.” If Diablo sounds darker than it’s ever been before, which says a lot for a series that’s long epitomized grim-dark video games, that’s by design. Blizzard intends Diablo V to feel bleak and hopeless, which can make every win shine brighter. “We’re doubling down on the darkness,” says Mueller. “Evil has infected everything. Civilization is devastated. The architecture is devastated. Even time has ravaged what’s been left behind. You have this apocalyptic vision of Sanctuary, and for a medieval dark fantasy, it is really compelling.” To that end, Diablo V is returning the franchise to a procedural dungeon system that’s been leveled up with modern software. There is a hundred years’ worth of horror that happened, which players will learn from the environment. “People will want to know what happened in the last hundred years as you’re exploring,” reveals Mueller. “The world is procedural; this is our third generation of procedural dungeon tech. People will get everything they got from the open world of Diablo IV in a dynamic way. You see stories of the past. Stories of survival and tragedy. This is where art is collaborating with narrative closer than ever.” Shely says that the world generation occurs as players move their caravan through the fog of war, like a rickety wagon in a frontier western epic. “The caravan itself moves through the world. It’s not a town that exists in a space. You’re taking your ‘town’ with you through this dangerous place that’s been transformed by the Dread Commanders. You explore, go through the world, and then return to that area with your caravan, and it’s been totally transformed.” While players might think work on Diablo V has just begun, it’s actually been in development for years. There is still more to learn about the game. It won’t release until 2029, which affords anyone still playing through Diablo IV more time to enjoy new, forthcoming content (like Season of Hell’s Legacy, which launches on September 15 to mark the series’ 30th anniversary). When Diablo V eventually arrives, it’ll be about two years into the next console generation. When Esquire asks how Blizzard is developing Diablo V on upcoming platforms, the team keeps mum. “Generally speaking, Blizzard wants to bring our games to as many players as possible,” says Shely, “and so we seek to make Diablo available on many platforms. You can see that with Diablo IV. You should expect the same with Diablo V. We want everyone to take on the Lord of Terror.” For now, all fans should know is that Diablo V is real, and it’s happening sooner than they might have assumed. And waiting for all of them on the long road ahead is one more fight with Diablo. Editor’s note: An earlier version of this story listed Jennifer Hepler’s name as “Jennifer Helper.” We regret the error. title: BlizzCon 2026 Opening Ceremony: Starcraft Returns, Diablo V Announced, Warcraft news and more - XBOX Wire
content: I’ve been at Blizzard a long time, and I’ve got a bunch of BlizzCons under my belt. Do you know how hard all these announcements were to hold in as we prepared for BlizzCon 2026? I can’t even believe this is real, man, like…okay, sorry, I’m locked in. Whether you’re watching it all unfold live or just catching up later, here is everything from the BlizzCon 2026 Opening Ceremony and where to go next for each one. From the farthest reaches of the stars, a new mission calls. StarCraft returns in 2030 as an original open-world shooter. There is really only one thing to say to that, and we said it from the stage and the halls in Anaheim, California: it’s about damn time. Diablo V is coming in Spring 2029, and it opens somewhere the series has never let us stand: after the loss. Sanctuary has fallen. Diablo has won. The question the game asks is what we become when the world we knew is gone. Closer to now, Diablo IV‘s Season of Hell’s Legacy lands September 15 (that’s this Tuesday!) to mark 30 years of Diablo. It brings back the Prime Evils, the Lord of Terror included, along with Deckard Cain, Nightmare Rifts, anniversary rewards, and gear pulled from every era of the series. A little further out, the Amazon joins as the next Diablo IV class in the first half of 2027, javelin in hand. And if you are at the show or playing from home, Moophisto has returned to terrorize the unsuspecting. He is as udderly malevolent as you remember. Heh. XBOX players can save 75% off Diablo IV and up to 30% on Diablo II: Resurrected content now through September 22nd. Everything coming to Sanctuary is on the Diablo website. Ten years of Overwatch, and the team spent its anniversary talking about what comes next. Season 5’s new Support Hero is Doctrine, a life-draining, vampire-inspired healer who sends out bat-like drones. You can play him at BlizzCon right now, and from home for a limited time. He arrives alongside major reworks for Sombra and Roadhog, plus a new map, Watchpoint: Grimsvotn. Season 5 also closes out The Reign of Talon, the first year-long story arc in Overwatch history, and it does not end quietly. The next Overwatch Spotlight follows in February 2027 with the team’s plans for the year. Two things worth clearing your weekend for: YOASOBI plays BlizzCon’s first-ever halftime show during the Overwatch World Cup, and LE SSERAFIM returns to the Main Stage as the closing act, with a new in-game collaboration live now. Then there is QuestWatch, a live Overwatch tabletop RPG one-shot written by Matt Mercer and the Overwatch Narrative team. For those playing on XBOX while you’re streaming at home: play one match to earn a Mythic Voucher and choose an eligible Mythic Hero Skin! More detail on all of it lives on the Overwatch website. Warcraft Goes Backward and Forward at the Same Time We are at the midpoint of The Worldsoul Saga. World of Warcraft‘s next major update, Eclipse (12.2), has Xal’atath closing in on Azeroth’s Worldsoul, and where that goes is up to us. We also got a look at The Last Titan, the final chapter of the Saga, which brings more than two decades of Warcraft storytelling to a close and sets up whatever comes after. More on that early next year. Then a genuine surprise: for the first time in over 23 years, there is a new Warcraft III: Reforged story. The Forsaken Kingdom campaign takes you back to the fall of Lordaeron and its turn into the Undercity, and it ships with the 3.0 update, which brings a substantial graphics overhaul and a revamped World Editor. It is playable today. We dropped it like a Beyonce album. Warcraft III: Reforged is available with XBOX Game Pass, so you only need to pick up the DLC to jump into the new campaign And then we went home. World of Warcraft: Forever is a third way to play alongside Modern and Classic, set in the Vanilla era, with room to explore corners of Azeroth we never got to see the first time: three new zones, over 1,000 new quests, nine new dungeons, two new raids, and the new Skyborne race. It launches November 4, 2026, with Beta starting September 17. The full Warcraft rundown is on the Warcraft website. Hearthstone Opens a Journal and Meets the Old Gods The overhauled Journal pulls every quest, achievement, and event into one place, tied together by the story of each expansion. It keeps a record of where you have been and grows as you keep playing. Reign of the Black Empire hits the Tavern October 20 and takes Hearthstone to the earliest age of Azeroth, long before the Old Gods were imprisoned. Its new keyword, Assemble, merges two cards into a stronger one, which is going to produce some combinations nobody planned for. Before that, on September 22, Battlegrounds adds a new minion type called Aberrations, grown out of Old God corruption and experimentation. Looking further out, the Monk arrives in March 2027 as the game’s first new playable class in six years, fluid and adaptable in the way the class has always been. Xal’atath joins Heroes of the Storm on September 28, playable on the PTR starting September 14. This one belongs to those of you who never stopped playing. There may even be another hero ahead? What year is this? An animated series set in the world of Diablo is in development with Netflix. More on that later, and it is not the only thing taking shape. The BlizzCon livestream runs all weekend with deep dives, panels, and a halftime show, and the full schedule is on the BlizzCon site so you can plan what you want to watch. If you only take three dates with you: Diablo IV‘s Season of Hell’s Legacy launches on September 15, World of Warcraft: Forever Beta opens September 17, and Forever itself launches November 4.  Dude, we’re so back.

title: Diablo V Is Coming Out In Spring 2029 - Engadget
content: Blizzard also confirmed that a Diablo animated series is in development with Netflix. BlizzCon has brought some unexpected news for the Diablo franchise, including a spring 2029 release window for the next installment in the video game series, as well as a confirmation of an animated TV series adaptation in the works with Netflix. For the game, Blizzard's teaser video and article only hints at the story's continuation after the events of Diablo IV, but it looks like players will be thrown straight into hellfire. Like the Diablo V teaser, the confirmation for the animated TV show was equally light on details and we still don't know the release date or which animation studio is in charge of the adaptation. Blizzard said it will have more to share about the series throughout the development process and only hinted that "Sanctuary's darkness is spreading." For those who aren't devoted Diablo fans, rumors of a TV adaptation for the franchise have been circulating for a while. A report from 2020 hinted that a Diablo TV series would be done in an anime style and was in preproduction with Netflix in charge of distribution. Beyond the confirmation of the fifth major game in the franchise and a TV series, Blizzard also hinted at similar adaptations for its other popular titles, including Overwatch and Warcraft.

title: Diablo’s Next Era Revealed at BlizzCon 2026: Opening Ceremonies Recap — Diablo IV - Blizzard News
content:
Thirty years in, Diablo has never had more content ahead of it than now. During the BlizzCon 2026 Opening Ceremony, we offered the first glimpse of Diablo V (coming Spring 2029), announced a new animated series set in the world of Diablo in development with Netflix, revealed the Amazon class pack coming to Diablo IV in 2027, unveiled Season of Hell’s Legacy, and confirmed that Diablo IV is coming to Nintendo Switch™ 2. And we’re just getting started. The celebration continues throughout BlizzCon with developer panels, live gameplay, and more from across the franchise, including Diablo Immortal x Spawn. To rewatch BlizzCon 2026 Opening Ceremonies, you can watch our panel here: Celebrate 30 Years with the Season of Hell’s Legacy Diablo V is officially in development and coming Spring 2029. For the first time, players will enter a Sanctuary where Diablo has triumphed and its heroes have been defeated. At the heart of Diablo V lies a defining question: what must you become when the world has already fallen? Join us for Diablo V: Forging the Next Era panel on September 12, 1:45 p.m. PT for an early look at the world, classes and creative vision shaping the chapter of Diablo. You can also sign up for future updates at Diablo5.Blizzard.com. Sanctuary’s darkness is spreading. Blizzard and Netflix are developing a new animated series set in the world of Diablo, bringing the franchise to a new screen. We’ll have more to share as the series takes shape. Until then, stay awhile... and stay tuned. The Amazon is coming to Diablo IV in the first half of 2027. She hails from the island of Skovos, revealed for the first time in Diablo IV in Lord of Hatred. Her return preserves the disciplined, athletic, and highly trained warrior fantasy players remember while reimagining the class for Diablo IV. Across four gameplay archetypes—Champion, Skirmisher, Ranger, and Commander—the Amazon can wield the returning bow and javelin, which introduces an entirely new weapon type to Diablo IV. Get a closer look at the Amazon in the Diablo IV: What's Next panel on September 13, 11:00 a.m. PT. Additional class pack details will be shared at a later date. More than 130 million players worldwide have entered Sanctuary across the Diablo franchise. Now, three decades of darkness return in Season of Hell’s Legacy, a playable tribute to Diablo’s most iconic characters, foes, locations and loot. In Season of Hell's Legacy, the lost soul of Deckard Cain returns to guide you through an epic journey to redeem the dark wanderers from the torment of the Prime Evils. Confront the Prime Evils Baal, Mephisto, and Diablo, reclaim splinters of their souls, and bear the burden of one of the Splinters to assume a portion of their power. But remember: no demonic gift is bestowed without a steep price. Read more of the legacy the Burning Hells has wrought in our Season Overview blog here, and join us for the Diablo IV: What's Next panel on September 13, 11:00 a.m. PT. Hell has arrived on Nintendo Switch™ 2. The Diablo IV: Age of Hatred Collection is coming to Nintendo Switch™ 2 on September 15. The Diablo IV: Age of Hatred Collection bundles the base game, Vessel of Hatred expansion, and Lord of Hatred expansion. Plunder through the jungles of Nahantu and the far-reaching shores of Skovos to challenge the Lord of Hatred’s hold over Sanctuary on Nintendo Switch™ 2. Note: Nintendo Switch™ 2 supports mouse and keyboard functionality when plugged in via USB, Joy-Con™ 2 mouse functionality is not supported. The 30th anniversary celebration continues throughout BlizzCon weekend with panel highlighting the voice talent behind some of Diablo’s iconic characters and the making of Diablo IV’s cinematics. Join us live at the Anaheim Convention Center or watch from home on the following channels (exceptions noted below): The future of Diablo begins here! Host Johanna Faries sits down with the Diablo V development team to share an early preview of the game's story, world-building approach, class design philosophy, and the vision that will define the next era for Diablo. Lynch age 93 passed away peacefully on September 12, 2026, surrounded by her family and loved ones. Doris was a lifelong resident of Toledo, Ohio. Born to Raymond and Edna (Merry) Stewart in 1933, Doris was the fourth child of this union and the only girl. She loved climbing trees, peddling papers, playing baseball with her brothers, and sneaking to watch movies at the Avalon theater. Her first movie was Gone with the Wind. Doris leaves behind a beautiful living legacy: four generations of a family that knows how to love, support, and cherish one another because she showed us the way. Doris was known by many names, but her favorite was Nana. She was a grandmother to 17, a great-grandma to 22, and a great-great-grandma to 3. Over the years she cared for and welcomed a number of children into her home and into her life and counted them as bonus grandchildren. It did not matter who you were or your age, Doris would welcome you into her home as family and make sure you didn’t leave hungry. Before you would leave, she would point at you and say, “don’t take any wooden nickels”. Doris and her husband, Larry, were active in the Sheriff’s Auxiliary and the Glass City CB Club, her CB handle was “Ding Dong” because she was also the local Avon lady. She sold Avon for over fifty-years making many connections and new friends along the way. Doris was a volunteer at heart, taking children home from the St. Anthony’s Villa for respite, helping with her daughter’s Girl Scout troops, and in her later years sitting on the board of Neighborhood Housing as Secretary. Doris had many hobbies including collecting Shirley Temple memorabilia, watching Little House on the Prairie, and her love of genealogy, creating binders of the family’s history for several family members. But everyone knows her favorite hobby was collecting dolls…. LOTS of dolls. Doris loved to travel and camp with friends and family, sharing laughs, building memories, and singing around the campfire. Some of her favorite trips were to Englewood, Florida, Marysville to visit family and road trips to Maine and the Smoky Mountains with her son and daughter-in-law. Doris was preceded in death by her parents, Raymond and Edna; husband, Lawrence “Big Larry”; daughter, Linda; son, Lawrence “Little Larry”; siblings, William, Raymond, Harold, and Richard; son-in-law, Paul Peace; and dear friends, Lillian Dukeshire and Sheila Granata. Doris is survived by her children, Beverly (Paul) Dernier, Kathleen Hendry, Candy Brower, and Douglas (Cathy) Lynch; son-in-law, Michael Newton; brother-in-law, Frank Lynch; sister-in-law, Nancy Stewart; and cousin and dear friend, Martha Rea. Family and friends will be received at the Newcomer Funeral Home (Southwest Chapel) 4752 Heatherdowns Blvd., Toledo on Wednesday, September 16, 2026 from 3:00-8:00PM. Funeral services will be held on Thursday, September 17, 2026 at 11:00 AM. Interment will follow at Ottawa Hills Memorial Park. In lieu of flowers, donations can be made to Elara Caring Hospice.
